chief_complaint: recurrent ear infections and severe pneumonias since turning 6 months old
hpi_details: 10-month-old male presenting with his fourth episode of Streptococcus pneumoniae pneumonia and chronic otitis media. The mother notes he was completely healthy until about 6 months of age, at which point he started getting sick constantly. He has two healthy older sisters, but a maternal uncle died of severe pneumonia in infancy.
ideas: mother thinks his immune system is just immature
concerns: worried he will end up like her brother who passed away
expectations: wants strong antibiotics and tests for his immune system

investigation_events.title: Quantitative immunoglobulins and B-cell count
investigation_events.availability_message: The immunoglobulin levels and B-cell count are now available.

core_concepts: XLA is caused by a BTK gene mutation leading to failure of B-cell maturation, very low or absent circulating B cells, and markedly reduced immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE).
Infants are protected by maternal IgG for the first ~6 months, leading to a classic presentation of recurrent encapsulated bacterial infections starting between 6-9 months of age.
Treatment involves lifelong Intravenous/Subcutaneous Immunoglobulin (IVIG/SCIG) replacement.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: recurrent ear infections and severe pneumonias since turning 6 months old
Key HPI features: Male infant, asymptomatic first 6 months, then recurrent sinopulmonary bacterial infections. Maternal family history of early male infant death.
Objective/Exam findings: Absent or very small tonsils and lymph nodes.
common_misconceptions: Confusing XLA with SCID; XLA patients have normal T-cell function and combat viral/fungal infections normally (except enteroviruses).
Assuming recurrent ear infections in a baby are always just normal daycare exposures.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize the X-linked inheritance pattern and offer genetic counseling and carrier testing to at-risk relatives.
Administering live polio vaccine (though rare now) which can cause vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis in XLA.
management_principles: Aggressive antibiotic therapy for acute infections.
Initiate lifelong IVIG or SCIG replacement therapy.
Avoid live enteroviral vaccines (especially oral polio vaccine); obtain immunology guidance for vaccination planning.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 10-month-old male presenting with 4th pneumonia. Healthy until 6 months of age. Maternal uncle died of pneumonia in infancy.
reference_soap.objective: Fever 39.0C. Diminished breath sounds right lower lobe. Absent tonsils and cervical lymph nodes on exam.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Treat acute pneumonia with IV Ceftriaxone. 2. Quantitative immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE) and flow cytometry for B-cell count (CD19+). 3. Refer to Pediatric Immunology for lifelong IVIG therapy initiation and genetic testing for BTK mutation.

learning_objectives: Identify the classic 6-month onset window for XLA due to waning maternal IgG
Recognize the X-linked inheritance pattern (maternal male relatives affected)
Understand that B-cells and immunoglobulins are completely absent, requiring IVIG

teaching.one_liner: A genetic defect in males preventing B-cell development, leading to severe bacterial infections that start at 6 months when maternal antibodies fade.
differentials: Common Variable Immunodeficiency (usually presents later in life)
red_flags: Family history of infant male deaths from infection

must_ask.say: Was he completely healthy for the first few months of his life?

must_ask.objective: Determine family history indicating X-linked trait
must_ask.say: Are there any males on the mother's side of the family who had severe infections or died young?
What kind of infections does he mostly get? Are they mainly ear, sinus, and lung infections?
